content: Children who are up-to-date on well-child visits tend to experience fewer hospitalizations due to accidents and injuries. They also show higher rates of enrollment in preschool dental services. However, no significant effects were observed on immunization rates. Child health outcomes were not consistently measured across studies, and as a result, child health was excluded from the meta-analysis. Regarding caregiving outcomes, the effects of interventions aimed at supporting healthy socioemotional development and behavior were categorized and presented in terms of specific aspects of parenting. These included caregiving knowledge, caregiving practices, caregiver-child interactions, child maltreatment, caregivers’ mental health, and caregivers’ self-efficacy. For caregiving knowledge, two studies evaluated the impact of programs. Caldera et al. (2007) assessed maternal knowledge of infant development using the Knowledge of Infant Development Inventory, while Barlow et al. (2015) used a maternal-reported questionnaire designed by the authors. Caldera et al. found no significant effects on maternal knowledge, whereas Barlow et al. observed significant improvements in caregiving knowledge among mothers in the intervention group. However, unadjusted means and standard deviations were not provided, preventing pooled results from being calculated. The overall quality of evidence was graded as very low. In terms of caregiving practices, eight evaluations examined program impacts. Two studies used the HOME inventory (Caldera et al., 2007; Barlow et al., 2015), while three studies used the self-reported Parent-Child Conflict Tactics Scale (Jacobs et al., 2016; Fergusson et al., 2005; Caldera et al., 2007). One study generated two parenting practice scores through factor analysis of caregiver self-reported measures (Fergusson et al., 2005). The overall quality of evidence for caregiving practices was graded as low. For caregiver-child interactions, five evaluations assessed program effects. Dishion et al. (2008) created a composite positive behavior support score using items from the HOME involvement subscale and direct observation measures. Van Ziejl et al. (2006) assessed sensitivity, positive discipline, and negative discipline scores through direct observation during laboratory tasks. The overall quality of evidence for caregiver-child interactions was graded as very low. Regarding child maltreatment, two studies evaluated program impacts. Fergusson et al. (2005) examined parental reports of contact with child welfare services for child abuse and neglect but found no reductions in agency contacts. Jacobs et al. (2016) reviewed Child Protective Services records for substantiated child maltreatment reports but also found no significant effects. For caregiver mental health, four studies assessed intervention impacts. Two studies used the maternal self-reported CES-D scale (Barlow et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2009), and two used the Depression Anxiety and Stress Scales reported by primary caregivers (Hiscock et al., 2008; Hiscock et al., 2018). The overall quality of evidence for caregiver mental health was graded as low. In terms of self-efficacy, three studies evaluated intervention impacts. Caldera et al. (2007) measured maternal self-efficacy using the Teti Maternal Self-Efficacy scale, while Breitenstein et al. (2012) and Gross et al. (2009) used the Toddler Care Questionnaire. Both Caldera et al. and Breitenstein et al. found significantly higher self-reported self-efficacy scores among intervention group mothers compared to control groups. However, Gross et al. found no effects. Unadjusted means and standard deviations were not provided, preventing pooled results from being calculated. The overall quality of evidence for self-efficacy was graded as low. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential moderating effects of program intensity (infrequent contacts or less than three months versus regular contacts and longer than three months) and program delivery (individual versus group-based/mixed contacts). None of the pooled effect sizes for child and caregiver outcomes differed by program intensity or delivery. However, statistical power to detect subgroup differences was likely limited due to the small number of studies for many outcomes. There were no indications of adverse effects caused by caregiving interventions aimed at supporting children’s socioemotional and behavioral development. Costing data were not readily available, with only one study (Hiscock et al., 2018) reporting intervention costs. The mean costs of this trial intervention program were AUS$218 (AUS$208 to the government and AUS$10 to families) and AUS$682 (AUS$516 to the government and AUS$166 to families) per family in the targeted and combined arms of the intervention, respectively. In conclusion, the global evidence on caregiving interventions to support children’s socioemotional well-being and behavior during the first three years of life is primarily derived from high-income countries (HICs). Therefore, these findings cannot be generalized to lowand middle-income countries (LMICs).
